Senses.Explanation: The matter has no single fixed direction is a formal pivot in Chan addresses: after denying that fixed talk, questions, or verbal display can contain the matter, the cited hall speaker opens another line for questioning or provisional speech. Jianfu Chenggu says the matter has no single direction before opening it eight ways for the assembly. Xingyang Qingpou rejects talk about Chan and question-answer traffic, then pairs the phrase with 'principle comes out by a hundred paths' and invites questions. Fayun Datong Shanben uses it before admitting the ancestors' second-order gate and speaking east and west. Fotuo Xun uses it to qualify his denial that verbal performance can transmit the matter. The recurrent job is an explicit pivot, not a claim that every direction is equivalent.

Senses.Explanation: The disciplinary code is the body of monastic rules by which conduct is measured. Xuzhou Xingsheng defines carrying out what has been disclosed so that conduct does not go astray as ‘code’ (律). Guxue Zhenzhe cites its requirement that one who has received precepts remain under the conferring authorities, and Fayan Wenyi turns its rule about hearing ornaments through a wall into a public question about violation. Zhongfeng Mingben says Baizhang's monastic regulations drew on this code to establish ritual forms. The records also bend the category: Wuxie Lingmo answers whether he resides according to Chan or the code by saying that he neither keeps the code nor sits dhyana, while Dazhu Huihai warns that a code master can bind himself by keeping it. The rule remains concrete even when masters test what keeping it does.

Senses.Note: A distinct but thinly represented use: law as the state's regulatory authority.

Senses.Explanation: Disciplinary rules are the hard forms that regulate conduct; Chan records preserve them as rules that can be received, followed, broken, or falsely dismissed in the name of freedom. Zhongfeng Mingben criticizes people who break the disciplinary rules and violate prohibitions without fear, then later rejects the opposite error of making secondary observance into a fixed mechanism. His two warnings keep the rule hard without making it the whole Chan test. Zhuanyu Guanheng explicitly glosses the title Daily Disciplinary Rules as the ordinary forms for maintaining conduct in daily use so it is not lost. In a raised case, Shakyamuni Buddha says two monastics have violated the disciplinary rules; Poshan Haiming then reworks how their expulsion and the subsequent request for teaching would be handled. Biographies also record receiving, following, or refusing such rules as concrete acts rather than abstract category.

A Vinaya master is a specialist in monastic discipline who may serve as an ordination teacher or preceptor. The records say that Nanyue Huairang entered monastic life under Vinaya master Hongjing, that Huineng received ordination from Vinaya master Zhiguang, and that Zhantang went to Vinaya master Kang'an for full ordination. The Jingde Lamp Record also places Vinaya master Guangtong in an adversarial exchange with Bodhidharma, while Dazhu Huihai's record has Vinaya master Faming challenge Dazhu Huihai. Those exchanges make particular Vinaya masters opponents; they do not make every Vinaya master a foil by definition.
Senses.Note: Ordination teacher, discipline specialist, and interlocutor all concern the same institutional role. The hostile Bodhidharma narrative is one inherited deployment repeated across lamp recensions and counts once.

Senses.Explanation: To 見佛 is to see the Buddha, but the records repeatedly make the apparent achievement unstable. Lotus-Color Nun uses supernatural power to arrive first; the Buddha replies that she has seen his visible body but not his teaching body. Tianyi Yihuai says that the Buddha is not seen in any speck, then directs the assembly to the sun by day and stars by night. When monks ask about brushing away dust to see the Buddha, Shending Hongyin says that the Buddha too is dust, Dacheng Huiguo says that both brushing and seeing are already wrong, and Liangshan Shanji warns against blurred eyes. Asked why he sees the Buddha but does not bow, Xingkong Miaopu answers with two slaps and ‘A house does not have two masters.’ The phrase therefore names a live claim tested in public exchanges, not a guaranteed spiritual accomplishment.

Senses.Explanation: To see one's own nature. Zen records place this claim in transmission formulas, instructions, questions, and explicit challenges. Hongren links it with directly becoming a buddha; a text attributed to Bodhidharma says that seeking a buddha requires it. Huangbo Xiyun answers a direct question by refusing to make nature a second object seen by a separate seeing subject. Dahui Zonggao repeats that it is required for an unerring road and immediately asks which mind recognizes and which nature is seen. Zhongfeng Mingben says direct pointing is no longer direct once it enters speech or contrivance, while Yongming Yanshou says that once nature is seen, mind and the teaching remedies both cease. The phrase names a claimed recognition, but the records repeatedly test what the grammar of a seer looking at a separate nature would wrongly add.

Senses.Explanation: The faculty or nature of seeing, a noun phrase rather than the action of seeing one's own nature. Hanyue Fazang and Bore Gulin each quote an outside claimant who treats this seeing faculty as an unchanging witness that survives the destruction of a visible tile or stove; both speakers identify that claim as an error. Huanyou Zhengchuan groups the phrase with the nature of hearing and the nature of awareness, then says seeing and nature are not two separately visible things. This distinct segmentation matters because translating these passages as an achievement of seeing one's nature would reverse their grammar and hide the criticism.

Senses.Explanation: Chan records use this paired action as a banner for direct recognition and as a proposition that teachers immediately unpack, question, or test. Yunju Zhi equates nature with Buddha and says this is why the phrase is used; Huineng voices it as the wished-for result of hearing his words; Guizong Huicheng says the ancestral teacher came from the west only to state it. The records thus retain both its compact banner form and explicit internal explanations.

Senses.Explanation: The four ordinary functions of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, named together as a fixed sequence. Wuxiang warns that making an additional understanding out of them is far from the Way, yet elsewhere says the same functions are unobstructed. Langye Huijue calls them causes of birth and death. Zhongfeng Mingben says that mind itself is seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing and that one should not posit another seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing on top of them. Dazhu Huihai says a person is not bound by these functions or confused by surrounding objects. Huineng says the six faculties still see, hear, sense, and know without being stained by the many objects. Dahui Zonggao later quotes Vimalakirti's warning that seeking the teaching through these functions is not seeking it. The four actions are translated directly rather than replaced with a separate technical faculty.

Senses.Explanation: Seeing form, clarify the mind is a compact encounter formula that joins visible form to immediate recognition. Yunmen raises the paired formula as a question; later masters quote and test it in public addresses. The records do not treat it as automatically valid. Tian’an Sheng compares clarifying mind by seeing form to filling hunger with a painted cake, and Zhengfang asks why one would need it at all. Zen bends the formula into tested encounter language, not a prescribed inner procedure.

Senses.Explanation: One’s point of understanding is where one’s seeing or understanding presently stands, not mere eyesight. Huangbo Xiyun warns that having any fixed point of understanding puts a person among outsiders who delight in views. Tianyi Yihuai judges Kashyapa’s point untrue, while Yanduan calls an answer ‘also the elder’s point of understanding.’ In the repeated exchange with the Zen Buddha, an unnamed monk says that a point of understanding is present but a point of confirmation is not. Yushan Shangsi makes the parallel distinction ‘a point of understanding is present, but a point of use is absent.’ These predicates distinguish what is being said about one referent; they do not create separate senses.

Senses.Explanation: Seeing the tracks is the second oxherding stage: the seeker has found signs of the ox but has not yet caught it. Oxherding sequences place it after seeking the ox and before seeing or catching the ox. Their headings, prefaces, and verses describe tracks beside water or in wild country as an initial but incomplete disclosure. The stage explanations explicitly call it provisional and distinguish seeing traces from direct possession.

In the Guizong case an unnamed monk is struck precisely when he is about to open his mouth; in Xuedou Chongxian’s meeting with Zhimen, the second blow falls at the same instant. Yuanwu stops Kaifu Daoning as soon as he begins, while Dahui threatens a hot iron wheel at the mere move. Zen bends an ordinary bodily transition into the timed boundary where an answer is demanded, interrupted, struck, or forestalled.

Senses.Explanation: Chan records use this verb for an awakening event that breaks open in a person and, in direct address, for bringing listeners to that event. Lamp compilers narrate Guling Shenzan, Angulimala, an unnamed monk, and Ashvaghosha as persons who open into awakening after an encounter, words, or a sound. The actors undergo the event; they do not utter its lexical label. Yongming Yanshou stresses that the event admits no intervening instant, Mazu Daoyi uses the verb causatively for opening his listeners into awakening, and Zhongfeng Mingben speaks of a time when it occurs naturally in sustained inquiry. Intransitive and causative syntax retain one core event while changing who undergoes or brings it about.

Senses.Note: The stored biographies use the phrase for appointments, a first public teaching seat, and the gathering of students; it does not mean merely explaining a point in conversation.

Senses.Explanation: To begin teaching publicly marks the assumption of a public teaching seat, usually at a named monastery and often by invitation. Xuance returned to Jinhua and opened a large teaching assembly; Baoci Xingyan was appointed to begin teaching at the newly founded Baoci cloister. Yuquan Chenghao was invited to begin teaching at Dayang, while Dongshan Zibao began at Dongshan and Duliangshan Quanzhi was ordered to gather students at Changshou. The recurring frame is an institutional public beginning, not a synonym for speaking about the teaching.

Senses.Explanation: To disclose or show something, including instruction shown in a public interview. An unnamed monk asks Baizhang Yuansu to disclose the intention of the patriarch’s coming from the west and receives “the mud ox swallows the huge wave”; the named layman He Changbai asks Juelang Daosheng for instruction for the Fushan assembly and receives a verse about clouds and snow. In the Longtan–Tianhuang case, Longtan Chongxin complains that he has long attended without being shown the essentials of mind. Tianhuang Daowu lists raising a hand when tea was brought and lowering his head when greeted, then asks, “Where was I not showing you the essentials of mind?” (那裏不是與你開示心要處). The Blue Cliff Record's compiler narrates that Jingqing Daofu used a responsive dynamic to “show later students” (開示後學); Jingqing is the person described, not the utterer of that clause. The monastery manager Chengyi tells Jifei Ruyi that he has received Jifei’s disclosure (承師開示), treating Jifei’s reply as instruction already given. Request, act, repeated conduct, and received instruction are stages of the same showing, not different lexical referents.

Permission and prohibition name the paired work of allowing and barring under a rule. Yulin Tongxiu says that rigid attachment obscures the purpose of permission and prohibition and prevents recognition of what the Buddha established. Shishuang Chuyuan uses the pair for Linji's four selections, which open or bar according to the hearer's capacity. Zhongfeng Mingben refuses an appeal to permission, prohibition, keeping, and violation that would make them excuses for lawlessness. Yongming Yanshou also uses the pair for distinctions made within the teaching while saying that first-principle emptiness itself leaves no tracks. The pair thus serves both the precept rule and Chan's controlled opening and barring.
Senses.Note: The precept and Chan cases retain one paired operation—allowing and barring—applied in distinct settings; context alone does not prove two different things.
